name: Jade Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you're free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out of the house by six and at the Prairie Valley Electric yard by half past. We're rebuilding the old lines across the farm country west of town, the ones put up in the sixties, so it's setting new poles, framing them, and stringing new wire past fields I've known all my life. I'm an apprentice, which is a funny thing to be at 58, and I do a lot of digging and hauling, and I climb when the foreman lets me. I'm slow, but I don't quit.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Milking cows. My husband Malik and I ran his family's dairy for 32 years, and when our backs gave out and neither of our children wanted it, we sold the herd and leased the land to the neighbours. My son-in-law Wes is a line foreman over in the next county, and he said, Jade, you can lift a calf, you can lift a crossarm. I thought he was teasing, but here I am. The farm money's put away and the lease pays every year, so I work because I can't sit still and because I believe a person ought to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd say I never trusted it anyway. At the yard I'd tell Earl, he's 62 and the other old one on our crew, that we can stop listening to the young fellows going on about robots. I don't go online, I'd say it after prayers to whoever would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish what I started. I get through the apprenticeship, I work until 63 or 64, and I go home to Malik and the grandchildren. That's the life I had planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade keeps going as she is, learning the trade and working the lines out west. She'd keep her basic phone, which only makes calls, and keep the farm money and lease income exactly where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit relieved. I'm a creature of habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never trusted it. What made you distrust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My granddaughter showed me one of those chat programmes and asked it about milking. It told her cows should be milked once a day. I've milked twice a day for 32 years, and that was the end of my interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Prairie Valley that's changed with new technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They gave the foreman a tablet with maps on it. He still asks Earl which field gate is open, because Earl's lived out here all his life. The tablet doesn't know Henderson keeps his bull in the back pasture.

S0.say: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. I'd tell Earl at the yard and say it to people after prayers, since I don't go online.
S0.think: Privately she gets to finish what she started, working until 63 or 64 and going home to Malik and the grandchildren. That's the life she'd planned.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is, learning the trade on the western lines. Keeps her calls-only phone and leaves the farm money and lease income where they are.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, as a creature of habit.
S0.quote: The tablet doesn't know Henderson keeps his bull in the back pasture.
S0.fieldNote: Jade speaks in farm terms and judges technology by whether it knows what she knows. A single wrong answer about milking ended her interest in AI. Her belief that a person ought to work, not money, is why she's on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep working and learn what they have to, same as farmers always have. When the milking parlour got computers, we learned. I wouldn't be complaining in public, complaining never fixed a fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me. I'm the slowest learner on the crew already, and if the job fills up with screens, I'll be lost. I'm not afraid of hard work, I'm afraid of feeling stupid in front of 25-year-olds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade would wait and see what Prairie Valley actually brings in before doing anything. She'd ask Wes, her son-in-law, to show her any new system on a Sunday afternoon so she isn't learning it in front of the crew. She'd keep her money as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the bills, about my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers learned the computers in the parlour. How did that go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik learned them. I learned the cows. That's the truth of it, he did the screens and I did the animals, and it worked because we were a team. On a line crew I haven't got Malik.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the young ones on your crew would say about you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm a nice old lady who brings good bread. And that I'm slow on the new stuff. They'd be right about both, but I'd rather be known for the bread than for crying about change.

S1.say: I'd say people should keep working and learn what they have to, as farmers always have. Complaining never fixed a fence, so I wouldn't complain in public.
S1.think: Privately it bothers her, because she's already the slowest learner and screens would leave her lost. She's not afraid of hard work but of feeling stupid in front of young colleagues.
S1.do: Waits to see what Prairie Valley actually brings in before acting. Asks her son-in-law Wes to teach her any new system on Sunday afternoons so she isn't learning in front of the crew.
S1.feel: Uneasy, about her pride rather than her bills.
S1.quote: Malik learned them. I learned the cows.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line about working and learning hides a private fear of looking foolish. On the farm she split work with her husband, who handled the computers, and on the crew she has no partner like that. She'd turn to family for help quietly rather than ask at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, plain wrong, to put machines in place of people that fast. I'd say it after prayers and to anyone at the feed store. A man or a woman needs work to be whole, and the companies pushing this in two years don't care about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me more than I'd say out loud. Not the money, we've got the farm money and the lease. It's what happens to the young people around here with nothing to do, and to my grandchildren, and to a place like ours where everybody's work holds everybody else up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade would retire at 60 rather than work beside robots, and spend more time with her grandchildren. She'd lean on the mosque and her family, and offer to take in one of Wes's crew if they lost work. She'd keep the lease and leave the savings alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. This one feels like the world tipping over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. Two years isn't long enough to finish my apprenticeship, and it isn't long enough for families out here to change anything. Farming taught me you can't rush a calf, and you can't rush a town either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to do something with their hands and to stay close to family, whatever the machines do. And I'd tell them work is about more than money. I don't know if that would help, but it's what I believe.

S2.say: I'd say it's plain wrong to replace people with machines that fast, because a person needs work to be whole. I'd say it after prayers and at the feed store.
S2.think: Privately it scares her more than she'd admit, though not for money. She fears for young people with nothing to do, for her grandchildren, and for a community where everyone's work holds everyone else up.
S2.do: Retires at 60 rather than work beside robots and spends more time with her grandchildren. Leans on the mosque and her family and offers to take in one of Wes's crew if they lose work.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, as if the world were tipping over.
S2.quote: Farming taught me you can't rush a calf, and you can't rush a town either.
S2.fieldNote: Jade's alarm comes from her values about work and community, not from money, which is secure. Her objection is moral: people need work to be whole. With two years, she'd leave rather than adapt, and she turns to faith and family for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, but at least people can get ready. At the yard I'd tell the young ones to start learning a second trade. I'd say after prayers that families should pull together and not wait for the government to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me finish my apprenticeship, and that matters to me. I'd be 63 when it hits and nearly done anyway. But I'd still worry for the young ones, and for my grandson who wants to be a lineman like his dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade would finish her apprenticeship in two years and work until about 63. She'd put some of the lease income aside each year for her grandchildren's training, whatever trade they choose. She'd sit down with Wes and her daughter to plan for their family if his job changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it still sits on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your grandson wants to be a lineman. What would you tell him in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to go ahead and learn it properly, because somebody has to know how the lines really work even if a robot does the climbing. And I'd tell him to learn welding or something else too. You don't run a farm on one crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't want government to save people. What do you want instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprenticeships, real ones, and businesses that keep people on. Families looking after families. If the government wants to help, pay for training, not cheques for sitting at home.

S3.say: I'd say five years is still too fast but at least people can get ready. I'd tell the young ones to learn a second trade and say families should pull together rather than wait for government.
S3.think: Privately five years lets her finish the apprenticeship, which matters to her, and she'd be nearly done at 63. She still worries for young workers and her grandson who wants to be a lineman.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship in two years and works until about 63. Sets aside some lease income each year for her grandchildren's training and plans with her daughter and son-in-law in case his job changes.
S3.feel: Anxious, less than the fast picture but still heavy on her chest.
S3.quote: You don't run a farm on one crop.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Jade finish what she started, but her worry for the next generation keeps her anxious. Her traditional views come through clearly: training and apprenticeships, not cheques. She plans for her family rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for people who are willing to work. At the yard I'd tell the young ones to use it. After prayers I'd say we should be teaching our children trades now, not waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me much. I'd be retired by then, back on the farm with Malik, watching the neighbours' cows on our old land. My worry is still the grandchildren, and what kind of town they grow up in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade keeps going with her plan: finish the apprenticeship, work until 63 or 64, and retire. She'd keep putting lease money aside for the grandchildren's training and talk with her grandson about learning a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Better than the others, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten, I get to finish and go home proud. With two, I'm walking away from something half done. And the town gets ten years to find its feet instead of being knocked flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people in charge to do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the small companies and the co-ops going so there's work close to home. Help young people get apprenticeships. I don't know much about the big picture, but I know a town dies when the young ones leave.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time for people who are willing to work. I'd tell people we should be teaching our children trades now.
S4.think: Privately it doesn't touch her much, since she'd be retired on the farm by then. Her worry remains her grandchildren and the kind of town they grow up in.
S4.do: Keeps going with her plan to finish the apprenticeship and retire at 63 or 64. Keeps setting aside lease money for her grandchildren's training and talks with her grandson about a second trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, better than the other pictures but persistent.
S4.quote: I know a town dies when the young ones leave.
S4.fieldNote: Even with ten years Jade doesn't fully settle, because her concern is her town and grandchildren rather than her own job. She is honest that she doesn't know much about the big picture. Her ideas for help focus on local companies, co-ops and apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. It would knock the whole town flat before anyone could do anything. What would help is real apprenticeships for the young ones, companies that keep people on even when machines come, and families and congregations looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether work is just about money. For me it never has been. I've got enough to stop tomorrow, and I get up at five because work gives a day its shape.

headlineQuote: I've got enough to stop tomorrow, and I get up at five because work gives a day its shape.
portrait: Jade Khan ran a family dairy with her husband for 32 years, then sold the herd and became an apprentice lineworker at 56 on the encouragement of her son-in-law. She has a calls-only phone, distrusts AI after it got milking wrong, and believes a person needs work to be whole. Her money is secure from the farm sale and land lease, so her fears centre on her pride, her grandchildren and her rural town. The two-year AGI picture alarms her and pushes her toward early retirement and her family and faith, while longer timelines let her finish her apprenticeship but never fully settle her worry for the next generation.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would knock her whole town flat before anyone could respond.
whatWouldHelp: Real apprenticeships for young people, companies that keep people on when machines arrive, and families and congregations looking after each other.
